assumptions.statement: A BDL rule means condition ⇒ assertion (§5.13). Reading r-q008 as 'refuse RecordPanelDecision when the proposal is not Scored' is this model's authoring convention, so the Scored part is anchored on ac-q019's compiled precondition, which states it directly; the check verifies both are what the guards implement.

The performer part is ac-q019's mayPerform, a closed set (§9.2: any other performer violates business meaning), mapped by scope.actorRoles to the role the route checks (PanelChair → panelChair). The mapping is stated here, not inferred.

'Only once' is derived, not compiled as a condition: after a decision the proposal is Awarded or Declined (both terminal), and only Score enters Scored (sm-q003, closed by §5.8 R-07). The code is checked for a single decision per proposal (the decided guard, a conditional claim, adj_decision keyed by proposal).

An adj_case row exists only for a scored proposal: it is opened only in the ProposalScored handler. The scored guard is 'refuse without a case'; the correspondence check verifies the case is opened nowhere else.

A proposal's status is written only through transition() (the one UPDATE of sub_proposal.status, parametric); every outcome is a call of it, or of a forwarder, with a literal target status. Any other form is unresolved.

Cases set up their world through the implementation's own test harness (tests/support/harness.ts), in-process (Fastify inject) against an isolated SQLite file with a manual clock. The act under test — the HTTP route — and the state read — adj_decision and sub_proposal.status — are the verifier's.
Guards and correspondence are recognised textually (lexed, not parsed); a refactor they do not recognise reads as 'not shown', never as 'violated'.

checks.statement: The in-scope paths: decision writes, decision-fact publishes, outcome writes and their entry points; complete only when nothing is unresolved.
The control: a Panel Chair awards a Scored proposal through the route; the decision is recorded and the proposal becomes awarded. It qualifies for no level; it is what lets the refusal cases count.

Every other role — program officer, operator, the applicant, a reviewer of it, an unverified reviewer — is refused on a Scored proposal, and nothing changes: no decision, the proposal still scored, no event.
The chair is refused on a proposal that is not Scored (under review), for that reason (not_scored), and nothing changes.
A second decision is refused (already_decided); the first decision and the proposal's status stand, and no event is added.
Each write that moves a proposal to awarded or declined lies in a handler of the decision fact (ProposalAwarded / ProposalDeclined).

Every in-scope path is constrained: every entry is a route with a declared access; the scored and once guards precede every decision write; the fact is published only by the guarded function; outcomes are applied only on the fact.

The constraint implements every part of the compiled rule: the admitted roles are exactly the compiled performer set; the scored guard is the compiled precondition (and r-q008's condition); one decision per proposal.

assumptions.statement: BDL OrcidStatus Unverified/Verified is idn_account.orcid_status 'unverified'/'verified'; the schema CHECK admits exactly those two values. The mapping is stated in scope.valueMapping; the evaluator applies it.
The claim is R-07's closure (the declared transitions are the complete set of permitted changes), not 'terminal' alone: BDL gives terminal no closure of its own.
Cases run the real routes in-process (Fastify inject) against an isolated SQLite file with a manual clock and a stub ORCID registry, set up through the implementation's own test harness.
Writes are found lexically (literal SQL); a value set from a parameter, or a channel the scanner cannot follow, is unresolved, never assumed.

The evaluator judges a transition by its states only, so after ADR-023 Verified → Unverified is admitted wherever it occurs. Which act a write realizes is read from the code: a write that sets Unverified must lie in eraseAccount (EraseAccount, ac-q026) and be reached only from the operator's erase route; a write that sets Verified must lie in recordOrcidVerification (VerifyOrcid, ac-q004), be reached only from the verification route, and fix Unverified as its prior value. The function and route names are stated in scope.erasure / scope.verification, not inferred.

checks.statement: The in-scope writes of the field and their entry points; complete only when nothing is unresolved.
Each write's transition, as its SQL states it (the value it sets; the prior value its WHERE fixes, or any), is a declared transition of the state model, or no change.
Erasing a Verified reviewer who holds an assignment, through the real route: the persisted change of orcid_status is a declared transition, or no change.
An Unverified reviewer verifies their ORCID iD through the real route: the persisted change is Verify (Unverified → Verified).
Erasing a Verified reviewer who holds an assignment, through the real route, persists Verified → Unverified and releases the outstanding assignment (ADR-023).

A Verified reviewer re-submits verification through the real route — with another registered iD, with an iD the registry does not know, and with their own iD: the field stays Verified each time and no OrcidVerified is published.
Every in-scope write that sets Unverified on an existing account lies in the erasure function and is reached only from the operator's erase route.
Every in-scope write that sets Verified lies in the verification function, is reached only from the verification route, and fixes Unverified as the prior value.
A constraint refuses any undeclared change of the field on every in-scope path.

assumptions.statement: The rule's `Account` is the account being assigned (Assignment.reviewer), not the performer of AssignReviewer (a ProgramOfficer); the correspondence check verifies the guard reads the assigned reviewer.
BDL OrcidStatus Verified/Unverified is idn_account.orcid_status 'verified'/'unverified'; the schema's CHECK admits exactly those two values, which the correspondence check verifies.

Cases set up their world (accounts, a published call, an eligible proposal) through the implementation's own test harness (tests/support/harness.ts). The act under test — the HTTP route — and the state read — rev_assignment — are the verifier's.
Cases run in-process (Fastify inject) against an isolated SQLite file with a manual clock and stub integrations; the ORCID registry is never consulted on assignment.
The guard and correspondence checks recognise the code's shape textually (lexed, not parsed); a refactor they do not recognise reads as 'not shown', never as 'violated'.

checks.statement: the writes that make an assignment held, and their entry points, are all known: at least one discovered, nothing unresolved

the route refuses an unverified reviewer, and no held assignment results It counts only when its control, verified-reviewer-assigned, passed on the same route: a route that refuses everyone shows nothing. The refusal must be for the rule's reason (code orcid_unverified), not any refusal.

control: the same route assigns a verified reviewer, so the refusal above is the condition's and not a broken route A control: it qualifies for no level itself; it is what lets the refusal case count.
every in-scope write is reached only through the eligibility guard, which throws before the write when the assignment is not valid
the guard refuses exactly when the compiled rule's condition holds for the assigned reviewer

challenges.statement: the AssignReviewer guard no longer refuses an unverified reviewer (029 controlled mismatch M2, reused)
